title: The Maccabees (1 Maccabees 4:36–59)
hook: after a desecration, the temple is cleansed and rededicated, the feast Jesus later attends

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raphael, the guide nobody recognized, and your line was an angel on the road.

"And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch." That's John's Gospel, naming a festival without explaining it. Which feast, and what was being dedicated? The answer is in a book from a time the temple was taken from the people. A foreign king, Antiochus, had set an abomination on the altar and forced sacrifices the law forbade. A priest named Mattathias and his sons resisted, and in time his son Judas, called Maccabeus, led them. Now they've won, and they walk up to see what's left.

First Maccabees is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, and some Protestant Bibles print it among the Apocrypha. Judas says to his brothers, in effect: our enemies are beaten, let us go up to cleanse and dedicate the sanctuary. They climb Mount Zion and find it desolate: the altar profaned, the gates burned, shrubs growing in the courts like a forest or a hillside. They tear their clothes, put ashes on their heads, and fall on their faces. Grief first, then the work. They choose priests who had kept the law and take down the defiled altar. A striking detail: they don't know what to do with its stones, so they store them on the temple mount until a prophet should come and tell them. They don't pretend to an answer they don't have. They build a new altar of whole stones, make new holy vessels, light the lamps on the lampstand, set out the bread, and early one morning offer sacrifice with songs, harps and cymbals while the people fall on their faces and worship. Then Judas and the congregation decide the days of the dedication should be kept every year, for eight days, with joy and gladness. That feast is Hanukkah, the Hebrew word for dedication, kept in Jewish tradition with lights for eight nights. Jewish tradition also tells a later story of a small jar of oil that lasted; First Maccabees itself doesn't tell it. And John's Gospel shows Jesus walking in that temple on that feast, in winter.

Think of something meant for good that got overgrown or misused: a room turned dumping ground, a morning hour lost to your phone, a friendship gone sour, a habit that used to be prayer and is now just noise. Let yourself be sad about it first, like the Maccabees, then choose one thing to clear and give back. If you pray, give it back to God in your own words; if you don't, just name what it's for again.
Hanukkah. Dedication: the feast that remembers the temple cleansed and its altar rededicated, the feast of the dedication John's Gospel names.
Your line: rededicate. What was overgrown can be given back. That's day seven hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Jews keep Hanukkah for eight nights by lighting a menorah; Christians meet the feast in John 10:22, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians read 1 Maccabees as scripture, while some Protestants read it among the Apocrypha.

chat.meaning: First Maccabees tells of the sanctuary cleansed and a new altar dedicated, with eight days kept every year. Hanukkah means dedication.

Maccabeus.meaning: the name given to Judas, who led the resistance

Antiochus.meaning: the foreign king who defiled the temple's altar

Mattathias.meaning: the priest whose sons resisted Antiochus

Hanukkah.meaning: Hebrew for dedication: the feast of the rededicated temple

sources.quoted: And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch.

notes: All of 1 Maccabees is paraphrased; the writer was not certain of the exact KJV Apocrypha or Douay wording.
'Hanukkah means dedication' is the standard sense of חֲנֻכָּה and matches John's 'feast of the dedication'; confirm under the claims rule.
The oil story (Talmud, Shabbat 21b) is described only as 'a later Jewish tradition' that 1 Maccabees doesn't tell; confirm this framing is respectful to Jewish readers.
'Jews keep it to this day, lighting lights for eight nights' is a neighbor's practice, described briefly; confirm.
Canon: 1 Maccabees in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; 'some Protestant Bibles print it among the Apocrypha'. Confirm.
Antiochus's desecration summarized from 1 Maccabees 1:47, 1:54; Judas called Maccabeus from 2:4.
Carry suggests lighting one light for eight nights (the outline's practice); not a Hanukkah ritual imposed on Christians. Confirm tone.
Editor pass: 'as if every reader would know' cut; 'Jews keep it to this day' (not in the cited text) changed to 'Jewish tradition keeps it'.

Audit: hook said the resistance was 'led by Judas'; 1 Maccabees 2 has Mattathias and his sons begin it, with Judas leading after his father's death (3:1). Now 'a priest named Mattathias and his sons resisted, and in time his son Judas, called Maccabeus, led them'; source 1 Maccabees 2:1–5, 3:1 is covered by the paraphrase entry.
